modules.title: 01 | Hostile Environments and Main Threats
modules.body: Module 01 \| Hostile Environments and Main Threats The security conditions in a country can vary greatly between locations and activities. It is an operating context where staff may be exposed to violence, terrorism, serious crime, unrest or limited emergency support. Learn how these threats affect actual tasks. Learning outcome: Distinguish threat types, identify exposure and protection gaps, and decide whether to proceed, change or suspend an activity. ## 1.1 \| Understand the high-risk operating environment The risk can change from one street or time of day to another. A visitor may attend meetings in a functioning city centre and then inspect a remote historical site. The city may have staffed hotels and medical care, while the outskirts face checkpoints, explosive remnants or limited rescue. The practical assessment starts with an activity: where will you be, for how long, with whom, and how might harm reach you? A meeting room, an exposed roadside survey and an independent visit each bring different exposure and available protection. HEAT teaches you to connect information about threats to the activity you actually plan to undertake, using current conditions along your route and at the destination. Reference map: Control Risks, RiskMap 2026 ([publisher's 2026 map information](https://www.controlrisks.com/jp/riskmap/maps)). Observe: What other local information is needed for this activity or road? Act: Verify current local threats, exposure, protection and emergency access before deciding to proceed. The map is a dated reference, not a live movement clearance. ## 1.2 \| Recognise the five main threat groups Armed conflict, terrorism, serious crime, civil unrest and environmental hazards produce different kinds of harm. Fighting can make access and medical transfer unreliable. A bombing can produce blast injury, fragments and a crowd surge. Criminal violence may involve robbery or abduction. A demonstration may become dangerous through confrontation or blocked exits. Imagine visiting an exhibition while a gathering develops outside. First check whether access is being restricted and whether you can leave safely. If glass breaks after an explosion, your response must change to protecting yourself from physical danger. Learners should understand how each threat could actually cause harm. Learners need to understand how that threat may actually affect them. ### Turning a security warning into a decision One visitor encounters a demonstration near an archaeological site, another faces an armed robbery, and a field researcher notices possible unexploded ordnance. Each situation calls for a different immediate protective decision. During unrest, the crowd and usable exits matter. In armed robbery, protecting life takes priority over recovering property. With a suspected explosive remnant, the essential decision is not to approach or disturb the item. The control must match the way harm may occur. Communication helps report an incident, structural protection reduces exposure to gunfire, guards manage access, and insurance can support costs after an event. Choose each measure for the problem it can actually address. ## 1.3 \| Judge whether threat information is useful People receive information from different sources: forwarded videos, official restrictions, security notices, hotel staff and witnesses. Check what each source actually confirms. Check when and where a video was made, whether the incident has been independently verified and whether it affects your planned activity. A road authority can confirm a formal closure; a driver can report the section personally travelled; a hotel may know its own access arrangements. No single source necessarily understands the whole area. Keep confirmed facts separate from rumours. Evidence of a nearby immediate threat may still justify a low-risk protective action while more information is checked. ### Two conflicting sources: what should happen first? A host emails that a visit will proceed, while a social-media video claims the historic site is closed and arrests have begun. The video is undated. The host knows the visit plan; current access restrictions may require confirmation from official sources. Separate the questions: where and when was the video recorded; is entry officially permitted today; does the event actually affect your activity? Postpone entering the affected area while you check the information. Pause entry where appropriate, seek a relevant official notice and check reliable recent information. If the video turns out to be an old event from another city, reassess the visit on current evidence. ## 1.4 \| Separate threat, exposure and vulnerability Threat, exposure and vulnerability explain different parts of a safety problem. Threat describes what may harm people. Exposure describes when and how they could encounter it. Vulnerability describes limits in protection, assistance or escape. During unrest, somebody already inside a usable building may have less exposure than a person crossing between groups of demonstrators. A companion who cannot walk quickly, or an accommodation building with blocked exits, has additional vulnerabilities. Travellers can start with a few practical questions. Ask which element can realistically change: stop unnecessary exposed activity, choose a more protected position, change the visit or improve essential support. Simulated training scene \| 1.4 Distinguishing threat, exposure and vulnerability when a station exit closes. Observe: How does a closed exit change the team's route and exposure? Which unverified step-free routes, companion mobility needs and pickup arrangements increase vulnerability? Act: Confirm a usable exit and accessible route with station signs or staff, agree on a safe pickup point, and hold movement until everyone can reach it together. Do not send anyone alone through an unknown passage. ### How a low-risk meeting becomes a much more exposed activity The same business visitor attends a meeting in a well-managed hotel in the morning and is unexpectedly invited to inspect a private property near a restricted border area in the afternoon. The distance from medical care, access rules and available protection have changed. Recheck the arrangements at the new location. Before asking whether to “continue the trip”, distinguish the essential business objective from the new activity. It may be reasonable to decline an unverified site visit and still attend an authorised meeting. An unverified site visit can be deferred while an authorised meeting still goes ahead. ## 1.5 \| Test protection by function, not appearance A fence, guard, CCTV system, fire exit and substantial structural wall do different jobs. A fence manages entry; physical ballistic protection requires suitable structures. Cameras record activity, while injuries require medical support. A thick-walled room may offer protection from external violence yet be unsuitable when smoke is spreading inside. Travellers can check usable exits, staffed locations and possible internal protection. Business visitors should also understand site alarms and access controls. When somebody says an area is safe because a guard is present, ask what protection that guard actually provides and what occupants must do when danger develops. ## 1.6 \| Recognise when the level of risk changes Security conditions can change within a single day. A hotel area that is calm in the morning may face restrictions by afternoon. A public attraction open yesterday may close because of nearby violence or an emergency. After a disruption, check which activities can still proceed safely. If fighting starts near a planned inspection point, check whether the exposure has increased and whether existing protection still works. A business appointment can sometimes be changed to a remote meeting; a sightseeing stop can be dropped. Stopping part of the plan before the situation deteriorates can preserve more options than waiting for a formal crisis declaration. ## 1.7 \| Prepare actual protection and emergency capacity Equipment has a specific protective purpose. A construction helmet protects against workplace hazards. Test satellite messaging before departure and confirm active service. Check medical access directly, alongside insurance arrangements. For a visitor, essential preparation may include lawful identity documents, necessary medication, an offline language and medical card, suitable communication and knowledge of the site's immediate hazards. An industrial visit may add personal protective equipment and formal entry training. Carry equipment suited to the actual task and the local rules. Unfamiliar specialist equipment may introduce new risks when people have not been trained to use it. ## 1.8 \| Decide whether to proceed, modify or stop A well-judged decision may be to proceed, adapt the activity or stop the exposed part. Make the choice based on the actual conditions. Suppose a visitor finds a suspected unexploded item in a recently contested area. The price of the entrance ticket is irrelevant: stop approaching and leave assessment to qualified specialists. If the problem is merely a late vehicle, waiting in an appropriate staffed location may be enough. Different conditions require different actions. The outcome of this module is the ability to explain what condition has failed, what will change and why that decision is safer than simply following the original schedule. ### Field tool \| From hazard to action | Hazard | Immediate priority | | --- | --- | | Fighting near the site | Suspend exposed work and use genuine protection | | Crowd forcing an entry | Control access and move staff to a protected area | | Suspected explosive item | Do not touch; withdraw and refer to specialists | | Emergency services unavailable | Reduce hazardous activity and arrange realistic support | Explain the threat, how harm could occur and the action that will protect the person. Simulated training scene \| 1.8 Deciding whether to proceed, modify or stop work. Observe: Which exposure and protective conditions are visible, and which essential facts—hazard clearance, lawful site access and specialist response—cannot be verified from the image alone? Act: Suspend affected work while critical conditions remain unverified. Stay clear of any suspected hazardous item; do not approach, touch or attempt to clear it. Resume or modify work only after authorised review of specialist findings. ### Case: a valuable visit with inadequate protection A host insists the delegation must inspect a restricted facility today and says “local people will look after you.” Without confirmed access rights, recent threat information and practical emergency support, that statement cannot demonstrate readiness. Consider whether the required information can be obtained through a video inspection, a presentation in an authorised public area or a later verified visit. A useful decision identifies what work can still proceed, what exposure cannot yet be accepted and what must change. Name the exact control or change needed. ## Module-specific assessment A visitor attends a meeting at a city hotel, then is invited to a restricted heritage site near a border area. Identify how exposure, authorisation and medical access change. Which activity should be deferred and which can still be carried out? Explain a decision using evidence using actual conditions for the activity. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, read the explanations and revisit the specific skill behind each missed question. modules.title: 02 | Preparing for High-Risk Operations
modules.body: Module 02 \| Preparing to Enter and Operate in a High-Risk Area Preparation means making sure people can perform the task, protect themselves and obtain real support if something goes wrong. Focus on the activities, threats and practical support available. Learning outcome: Complete an operational readiness check for yourself or a small team and identify conditions that prevent safe entry. ## 2.1 \| Define the task and entry conditions Begin by deciding what the trip needs to achieve. A visitor may want to see a historic site, a business traveller may attend a meeting, and an engineer may inspect a remote installation. Their objectives differ, but the safety question is the same: what is essential, what can change, and which areas should not be entered? A site advertised as open may still be surrounded by checkpoints, restrictions, unexploded ordnance or limited medical support. Check whether the activity is lawful and actually permitted, and confirm any relevant access permissions. For inspections, identify any additional access permissions and protection requirements. Write down what the activity permits, what change should stop it and what people can do safely if it stops. If the activity stops, the group should already know where and how to continue safely. ### Invitation, activity and authorisation are different A short-term visitor receives an invitation covering a historic site and an industrial facility. After arrival, the host suggests photographing a border-controlled area. Check entry, photography and professional activity permissions separately from the invitation. These permissions may come from different bodies. Do not enter an uncertain restricted area first and try to settle the question afterward. Defer the new visit, remain within the authorised scope or obtain clarification through legitimate channels. ## 2.2 \| Learn site emergency procedures Many people first ask about emergency procedures after entering a hotel, historic site or compound. When something happens, they may have no time for a full briefing. Within the first few minutes, know who manages the location, which exits actually work, what internal areas may offer protection and how a fire alarm differs from an external security warning. A fire inside a building often calls for evacuation under the building's emergency instructions. Violence outside may make staying in a usable protected area safer. One rule such as 'always meet at the front gate' cannot manage both conditions. At a venue that offers no briefing, identify the usable stairs and exits yourself and identify staffed points where you can request help. Confirm that the facility is actually operating. ## 2.3 \| Check documents and lawful authorisation A passport, entry permission and any site-specific permits should all be checked. Verify entry permission, the stated purpose of your stay and any permits needed for archaeological, border, research or industrial sites. Restricted areas may require a separate permit. Consider a second question: if you were taken away, could somebody outside establish who you are? Keep secure copies of your identity page, visa or entry record, essential medical facts and an activity summary. A trusted receiver should hold a protected backup with your consent. Do not put sensitive scans into an unrestricted group chat. A zippered inner pocket or separate secure compartment can hold a lawful ID copy, emergency language card, medication details and modest emergency cash if permitted. The inner pocket keeps lawful emergency items separate from the main bag. Do not resist a search to protect these items. ### Identity records for an emergency outside contact If a passport and phone are retained, the person may be unable to explain even the spelling of their name. Before departure, arrange for one trusted external receiver to hold enough protected information to assist verification: identity-page copy, visa or relevant permits, lawful purpose of visit, actual accommodation and receiving organisation, a recent photograph and essential medical considerations. Disclose complete identity documents only to appropriate authorised consular, legal or official channels, not to every group chat. Separate paper copies or secure inner pockets reduce the chance of losing everything together. They must never be used to conceal prohibited items or justify sudden reaching during an armed search. The external backup remains valuable even when all personal belongings are taken. ## 2.4 \| Establish health and medical support Medical planning includes confirming available treatment, transport and actual travel time. The nearest clinic may lack the ability to treat serious trauma, and an ambulance may be delayed by insecurity, road restrictions or lack of fuel. Bring prescribed medicines in accordance with professional advice and local rules, with suitable documentation and a reasonable allowance for delays. Keep critical medicine accessible where lawful. Confirm the realistic availability of care and medical transfer. Confirm how emergency transport will be arranged, alongside the insurance cover. For a short-term visit involving someone with a serious medical condition, adjust the location, duration or participants if the necessary support cannot actually be provided. ## 2.5 \| Prepare and understand protective equipment Protective equipment has specific limits. Construction helmets protect against specified workplace hazards. Ballistic and respiratory hazards require suitably rated equipment. Choose equipment according to the task, legal restrictions and user training. Choose according to what the activity exposes you to. An active industrial site may require safety footwear, eye protection and a formal briefing. In a city facing violent unrest, knowing where meaningful shelter is available may matter more than wearing inappropriate equipment. Check fit and condition, and do not carry devices whose use is prohibited or whose appearance may be misinterpreted at a checkpoint. Specialist equipment requires suitable training. ### Choosing equipment for the actual task A city meeting may require appropriate clothing, personal medicines, a working phone and backup power. Entry into an area with specific fragment or industrial hazards may require equipment selected by competent specialists and practical training. Use task-specific protection and confirm any specialist requirements before entry. Equipment can create difficulties of its own. Heavy loads reduce mobility, conspicuous items can attract attention, and unlawfully carried communication devices may lead to detention. Match every item to its protective function, your ability to use it, local rules and the task itself. ## 2.6 \| Test communications and emergency resources Loss of communication can mean several different things: a damaged phone, lack of coverage, overloaded networks or the confiscation of all equipment during detention. Plan a different response for each type of failure. For unavoidable remote activity, a lawfully permitted satellite phone or tested two-way satellite messenger may be appropriate. Confirm service coverage, activation, battery, actual message delivery and how the receiver will act. Agree who receives the alert and what assistance is realistically available. But if the traveller is taken into an unknown facility without a phone, the useful plan must operate without them. A trusted person outside should already have sufficient identity and last-activity information to begin tracing. Modules 05 and 10 show how to turn that into lawful consular and local enquiries. Simulated training scene \| 2.6 Backup communications at a remote worksite. Observe: If cellular coverage disappears completely, which pre-tested independent channel can deliver an alert, and who will acknowledge it and escalate a missed check-in? Act: Verify local legal requirements, activate and test the equipment before departure, and agree on the recipient, check-in schedule and overdue response. Restrict or postpone exposed work if essential communications cannot be established. ## 2.7 \| Consider physical readiness and stress Fatigue changes judgment. After a long flight, dehydration, disrupted sleep and a stressful inspection, people are more likely to misread instructions or miss a visible change. Preparation includes rest, adequate time and understanding the demands of the activity. Practise concise phrases for a tense encounter, such as asking for an interpreter, explaining before reaching for documents and stating a medical need. Practise them aloud before departure. Visitors may feel pressure to complete a once-in-a-lifetime visit or a rare meeting. When conditions deteriorate, reschedule the visit or choose a safer way to achieve the objective while alternatives remain available. ### Pre-departure reference \| Identity packet and essential local-language phrases A disappearance becomes harder to trace when nobody outside can prove who the traveller is or where they were last reliably seen. Keep one appropriate set of documents with the traveller and a protected backup with a trusted, consenting receiver. The second set should contain enough evidence for consular or legal enquiries, not unrestricted access to private information. | Information | Traveller | Trusted external receiver | | --- | --- | --- | | Identity | Valid passport and lawful ID; limited permitted copies | Secure passport details, nationality, visa and relevant entry documents | | Activity | Actual access authorisation and necessary itinerary details | Last directly confirmed site, time, witnesses, organiser and lawful local support | | Emergency needs | Paper language card, essential medicine details and embassy contact information | Embassy/consular channels, qualified lawyer or lawful Fixer contact, and agreed escalation | | Evidence | Do not carry excessive sensitive documents | Preserve direct messages and witness accounts; label unverified clues separately | Zippered inner pockets or discreet, separate clothing compartments can provide a backup for lawful documents, a waterproof emergency language card, modest cash and essential medical details. Their purpose is to reduce single-point loss when a bag or phone is taken. They are not a method of hiding prohibited items, defeating lawful searches or maintaining covert communications. Never escalate a confrontation to protect belongings. ### Minimum local-language practice \| Arabic reference Before travelling, learn how to ask for food, water, a doctor, medicine, an interpreter, your embassy and your family. These examples use Modern Standard Arabic. Romanisation is approximate; a competent local speaker should check pronunciation, dialect and relevant gender forms, and the traveller should keep offline audio if possible. | Meaning | Arabic reference | Approximate pronunciation | | --- | --- | --- | | I don't understand Arabic | لا أفهم العربية | Lā afham al-ʿarabiyya | | Please speak slowly | تكلم ببطء من فضلك | Takallam bi-buṭʾ min faḍlik | | I need help | أحتاج إلى مساعدة | Aḥtāju ilā musāʿada | | I need water | أحتاج إلى ماء | Aḥtāju ilā māʾ | | I need food | أحتاج إلى طعام | Aḥtāju ilā ṭaʿām | | Where is the toilet? | أين الحمام؟ | Ayna al-ḥammām? | | Where is the hospital? | أين المستشفى؟ | Ayna al-mustashfā? | | I need a doctor | أحتاج إلى طبيب | Aḥtāju ilā ṭabīb | | I need my medicine | أحتاج إلى دوائي | Aḥtāju ilā dawāʾī | | I need an interpreter | أحتاج إلى مترجم | Aḥtāju ilā mutarjim | | I want to contact my embassy | أريد الاتصال بسفارتي | Urīdu al-ittiṣāl bi-sifāratī | | Please notify my embassy | أرجو إبلاغ سفارتي | Arjū iblāgh sifāratī | | I want to contact my family | أريد الاتصال بعائلتي | Urīdu al-ittiṣāl bi-ʿāʾilatī | | Why am I detained? | ما سبب احتجازي؟ | Mā sabab iḥtijāzī? | | I am from China (example) | أنا من الصين | Anā min aṣ-Ṣīn | Practise at least five phrases without looking at your phone. For destinations where Arabic is not appropriate, replace the entire card with the relevant local language instead of using these expressions universally. ## 2.8 \| Carry out a final task-readiness check The final readiness check should include a short exercise in responding to failed arrangements. Imagine the venue closes, the original transport disappears, someone is held for questioning or a phone is confiscated. Can you explain the first safe action for each situation? Bring together lawful identity documentation, the language card, necessary medicine, knowledge of local safety procedures and an external GOTWA arrangement. The receiver needs enough facts to act if you disappear; you need to know how to request water, a doctor, an interpreter and consular contact if your equipment is gone. Before departure, check that principal hazards have practical controls, stop conditions are clear, and the external receiver can act if you lose contact. ### Operational readiness checklist | Area | Confirm | If not ready | | --- | --- | --- | | Task | Scope, work area, limits and stop criteria are clear | Suspend or reduce the activity | | People | Fitness, training and assigned roles match the task | Reassign or train personnel | | Equipment | Protective, medical and communication items work and can be used | Repair, replace, test or train | | Site | Access, protection, alerts and emergency procedures are known | Brief and practise before entry | | Rescue | Medical and emergency support can actually respond | Reduce exposure or change the task | Two-image observation exercise (both are simulated training scenes): Image one tests entry readiness: Which permissions, personnel capabilities and stop-work conditions cannot be verified from an image alone? Action: confirm them before entry and postpone if a critical condition is missing. Image two tests emergency capability: Can the image prove that communications, medical reception and evacuation are operational? Action: test communications and confirm reception, transport and backups; reduce or postpone the task if checks fail. ### A ten-minute rehearsal for an unexplained disappearance Ask one member of the group to imagine that their phone has been confiscated. Another acts as the person outside. Without calling the missing traveller, the receiver must explain how identity can be established, what the last independently confirmed location was, which lawful institutions can receive the record and what threshold triggers action. If the required evidence is missing, fix the handover before departure. Now change the case: there is no mobile coverage for several hours. Check the lawful backup communications and realistic check-in arrangement. Follow the agreed procedure for scheduled signal gaps. Witnessed detention requires immediate external action. ## Module-specific assessment Imagine a traveller's passport and phone are both retained at an inspection point. Without the person's device, can the agreed receiver verify identity, lawful purpose and the last confirmed location? Which prepared documents, local-language phrases and lawful assistance channels would make a practical difference? ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, read the explanations and revisit the specific skill behind each missed question. modules.title: 03 | Situational Awareness and Personal Security
modules.body: Module 03 \| Situational Awareness and Personal Security Focus on the changes that affect your immediate safety. Learn to notice changes that matter, reduce exposure and act before a situation becomes an immediate threat. Learning outcome: Recognise warning signs at a compound, worksite or public location and change your actions using direct observations and verifiable information. ## 3.1 \| Stay aware of the operating environment Situational awareness starts with knowing the space around you. It begins by understanding the place you are actually using: the entrance, a second usable exit, the staffed area and what normal activity looks like. Cooper's colour code can be a useful memory aid for your attention and actions, as a prompt for managing your own attention. White means being absorbed in a phone or conversation. Yellow means going about normal activities while remaining aware of the environment. Orange means a specific relevant change requires attention and a possible adjustment. Red means an immediate danger calls for protective action. For example, a traveller enters a restaurant, identifies the exits and then eats normally. Later, people rush inside and staff close the street-facing doors. Move away from glass and check whether the building remains usable while the situation develops. ## 3.2 \| Know what normal looks like You cannot notice a meaningful change until you understand the normal pattern. A market usually closes at six, but several shops close at three. A historic site's normal entrance suddenly stops admitting visitors. Traffic and pedestrians begin moving in an unusual direction. These changes can justify pausing an activity and checking what has happened. A festival, power failure or temporary restriction may explain what you see. Culture and local routines matter: unfamiliar clothing or behaviour must not become a proxy for suspicion. Ask whether the change affects your access, companions, current position or ability to leave safely. Pausing the movement and checking a genuine alternative can be sensible even when the cause later turns out to be harmless. The immediate task is to avoid unnecessary exposure while the situation is being clarified. ### What change is important enough to alter your activity? Pay attention to changes that affect your own route or activity. A stronger indicator is a cluster of changes affecting your immediate environment: an entrance unexpectedly closes, staff leave their posts, access is restricted and pedestrians begin moving away from an area. Several changes occurring together can justify stopping your approach and choosing a less exposed position. When the situation is uncertain, pause optional activities and keep direct observations separate from assumptions. ## 3.3 \| Recognise concerning behaviour Seeing the same person twice is common at transport hubs and attractions. Airports, stations and popular sites naturally bring people together. More concerning patterns include repeated questions about your room or departure time, sustained attention to restricted entrances, attempts to change a verified meeting point, or unwanted following combined with blocked movement. Suppose somebody says a meeting has moved to a private office and refuses to identify the organiser or let companions attend. While you are free to decline, remain in a staffed area and verify the change. Do not follow the person into isolation merely to determine whether their story is true. Describe what you actually saw: where, when, words used and actions taken. Avoid assumptions based on ethnicity, accent or appearance. Do not try to test suspected followers through speeding, dangerous turns or isolated streets. ## 3.4 \| Avoid fatigue and false familiarity Fatigue narrows attention. After long flights, inadequate sleep, dehydration or a demanding field visit, travellers may miss an obvious closure, misunderstand a warning or fail to notice that a driver has made repeated errors. The practical response is to adjust the plan: rest, replace a fatigued driver, change the schedule or reduce the number of activities. If the driver is exhausted, stop for rest or change drivers. Familiarity creates its own risk. Check current instructions at each passage through a checkpoint. Today's actual restrictions and observations are more important than yesterday's routine. Stay aware of changes that affect movement, access and personal safety. ### Fatigue can make situational awareness a performance After several transfers and little sleep, three business travellers join an evening visit. One continuously checks their phone map but overlooks officers restricting the entrance. Fatigue reduces attention and judgment. Reduce optional activities, avoid making one exhausted person responsible for every decision, and arrange actual rest. Reserve focused attention for important changes and transitions. Renew attention at meaningful points: entering a new venue, receiving a warning, noticing an altered access arrangement or detecting a change in nearby behaviour. ## 3.5 \| Use a position that offers protection When direct danger develops, people often approach a window or doorway to find out what happened. During gunfire, explosions or crowd violence, this instinct can increase exposure. A curtain or lightweight divider may conceal someone from view without providing physical protection from projectiles or fragments. Consider shots outside a hotel meeting room. Move away from windows and open access points and use a more substantial protected position if available. Do not cross a long exposed lobby simply because it looks like the normal route to safety. Wait for a usable and safe route before moving outside. Fire inside the building presents a different problem. A location that protects you from outside violence may become untenable if smoke spreads. The first decision always depends on the immediate source of danger. Simulated training scene \| 3.5 Choosing a protected position. Observe: Which positions may be exposed near windows, entrances or open passages? Which barriers require more information about their actual protective capability? Action: When gunfire presents an immediate threat, move away from glass and exposed positions and use substantial structural protection where available. Choose a position with substantial structural protection and assess the route to it; lightweight partitions offer little protection against gunfire. ## 3.6 \| Limit unnecessary information exposure Provide your legal identity when required, while limiting unnecessary public disclosure. Hotels and work sites require legitimate registration. What matters is limiting unnecessary public disclosure of the next destination, room number, staff identity, schedule and sensitive photographs. Information can be shared differently with different people. Keep your public sharing limited. Give the designated external receiver the identity and last-activity details needed to trace you in an emergency. The trusted receiver needs access to essential emergency information. Avoid keeping every passport copy, medicine note, emergency phrase and contact detail in one bag. Lawful, separated backups and a secure external copy reduce single-point loss. Use secure pockets only for lawful backup items and documents. ## 3.7 \| Handle unwanted approaches Unwanted approaches may sound helpful: “Your driver changed”, “The organiser is upstairs”, or “This is the shorter entrance”. If an arrangement changes unexpectedly, pause and verify it through a known contact. At a transport terminal, a stranger may know your surname and hotel because those appeared on luggage or an itinerary. Neither fact verifies the person. Remain where staff are present and confirm through the original booking or organiser. At a meeting venue, decline an unverified demand to enter an isolated room alone while the visit is still voluntary. If someone uses force, blocks an exit or displays a weapon, the circumstances have changed. A calm refusal is no longer a complete protective plan. Module 08 deals with forced control and detention. Scenario extension \| From an unwanted approach to an immediate armed threat: In the access-control situation above, you may still verify authority, decline entry and return to a staffed area. The following image presents a separate situation: an armed person threatening someone at a vehicle window. At that point, do not continue identity checks or arguments. Prioritise survival, avoid sudden movements and seek help once safely clear. Simulated training scene \| 3.7 An armed threat appears at the vehicle window. Observe: Which actions show that the person at the vehicle is making an immediate armed threat? Act: Prioritise life safety, keep your hands and movements visible, and do not suddenly reach for a phone or struggle over property. Once safely away, contact local emergency services and report your location, people's condition and what you actually observed. ### Following someone or simply walking in the same direction? A stranger leaves a gallery and walks in the same direction as you. Watch for repeated approaches, demands for personal information or attempts to isolate you. If the person repeatedly approaches, demands personal information or follows you into a staffed public venue, the situation deserves closer attention. Do not test the suspicion by entering an alley or improvising counter-surveillance. Do not confront someone alone. If the person tries to force you into another office or blocks your exit, the issue is no longer merely observation. Modules 04 and 08 deal with the escalation to coercion and loss of freedom. ## 3.8 \| Turn observation into protective action Awareness is useful only when it changes a decision. Imagine sitting in a cafe near a historic site when pedestrians suddenly run, road traffic stops and the booked vehicle cannot reach you. You do not know whether a security incident, fire or routine closure caused the change. First check whether the cafe itself remains usable, whether staff are present and which exits are genuinely open. If violence is outside, avoid leaving simply to find the driver. If smoke enters the building or attackers force entry, the earlier shelter decision must change. A useful mental check asks four questions: What did I actually observe? What remains unknown? Where is the immediate danger? Which action reduces exposure right now? Two-image observation exercise (both are simulated training scenes): Image one tests recognition of change and exposure: Which visible developments may affect access or safety, and what remains unknown? Action: stop non-essential movement into uncertain areas and verify from a safer position. Image two tests protective action: Which apparent routes have not been confirmed safe? Action: move people to a controlled area, account for them and notify the coordinator; resume movement only after checking conditions. ### A one-minute judgment exercise You are waiting inside a visitor centre. Staff say you must use a service door because a crowd is gathering near the front. Another guest claims the service door is a trap. You cannot verify either statement immediately. Check the identity of the staff member, whether the service door is available and whether the current lobby remains safe. You may be able to pause movement and verify. Fire or direct violence approaching the lobby would change that choice. The point is not guessing correctly afterward. It is avoiding unnecessary exposure when information is incomplete. ## Module-specific assessment At a public venue an entrance closes, staff leave their usual positions and people begin moving in the opposite direction. Separate direct observations from assumptions. Which activity should pause, and how could the team safely verify whether the change is routine before resuming? ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, use the explanations to find where your decisions were uncertain, then revisit the relevant course. modules.title: 04 | Cultural Awareness, Communication, and De-escalation
modules.body: Module 04 \| Communication, Culture and De-escalation A misunderstanding during a hostile encounter can quickly make people less safe. Learn to speak clearly, control your movements and recognise when a conversation is no longer the right response. Learning outcome: Handle difficult checks, disputes and confrontations without abandoning essential safety boundaries. ## 4.1 \| Respect customs without surrendering safety rules Effective communication helps prevent a manageable problem from escalating. A checkpoint officer, hotel employee, local guide and community representative may use different languages and work under very different pressures. A misunderstanding can turn a manageable access problem into a confrontation. Start by listening to the actual request. Ask what the person actually wants, and listen to the answer. At the same time, keep your own access and meeting arrangements within agreed, verifiable boundaries. When visitors are challenged over photography at a historical site, stop the disputed action and clarify what is permitted. If the encounter becomes physically threatening, immediate personal safety takes priority over further explanation. ## 4.2 \| Give one clear instruction at a time Long instructions are especially vulnerable to mistranslation during a crisis. “Everyone should stop going forward while I check whether we can use the rear entrance” can be turned into several contradictory commands. Use short statements with one main action: “Stop entering the hall.” “Move away from the windows.” “Do not open this door.” Ask someone to repeat what they will actually do, so you can check that the instruction was understood. Use a separate, clear instruction for stopping work, sheltering and evacuation. At a hotel or public venue, visitors may not know the local alarm signals. Identify those signals early. Clear, practised actions are more dependable under pressure than a long improvised speech. ### Learn phrases you can actually use without a phone During a checkpoint inspection or questioning, the interpretation app may be inaccessible and your device may have been taken away. Before entry, practise saying and understanding short local-language requests: “I do not understand”, “Please speak slowly”, “I need an interpreter”, “I need a doctor”, and “Please notify my embassy.” Keep an offline pronunciation recording and a discreet paper card. A generic translated phrase from the internet may be misunderstood in local dialect, so ask a competent local speaker to check it beforehand. Avoid asking for five different things in one sentence. First explain the communication problem. Pause. Request interpretation. If the situation permits, then ask a separate question about documents, procedures or medical needs. Clear repetition is more useful than speaking louder. Module 02 contains an Arabic example. ## 4.3 \| Work effectively through interpreters An interpreter must convey information accurately, not decide the outcome on behalf of either party. When several travellers speak at once and the interpreter adds opinions, nobody knows what was actually agreed. Choose one speaker and pause after each point. Repeat names, times, access permissions and amounts through the interpreter. Where possible, write down critical details to confirm they match. If the interpreter begins making legal promises or speaking beyond the agreed role, stop and clarify. Use the interpreter for communication and a qualified lawyer for legal advice. Formal detention, signing documents and legal procedures require suitable professional advice when available. Simulated training scene \| 4.3 Interpreter-mediated discussion. Observation: Which facts are most likely to be distorted when several people speak at once? Safe action: Appoint one speaker, verify locations, numbers and demands one at a time, and suspend negotiations if interpretation fails or threats escalate. ## 4.4 \| Control gestures and visible movements At an armed checkpoint, a rapid movement may matter more than your intended explanation. Reaching suddenly into a jacket for a passport can be misunderstood even when the intention is completely innocent. Keep your hands visible and move slowly. Explain before retrieving documents or opening a bag and wait for permission when possible. Avoid filming, pointing or having several people argue simultaneously. If you cannot understand a command, use a prepared phrase to request an interpreter or repetition. During a tense inspection, focus on controlled movements and clear requests. After reaching safety, seek legal or consular support for any procedural concerns. ### Your meeting location is part of your protection Two business visitors are waiting in a hotel lobby. The host unexpectedly asks one visitor to go alone to a basement office to sign papers and leave their passport behind. The proposed change would take the visitor away from the agreed public meeting place. While participation is voluntary, ask to use a staffed area and verify the procedure before proceeding. Do not hand over the visitor, passport and phone together merely to appear cooperative. If the situation escalates to physical control or threats, insisting on the original meeting rules is no longer the immediate priority. The person controlled should minimise provocative movements; the companion still free should preserve the last confirmed time, place, people involved and demand for use in lawful external enquiries. ## 4.5 \| De-escalate an angry complaint A historic site may refuse entry despite a paid booking, or local residents may object to a visiting vehicle. Ask what specifically needs to change, stop the disputed activity and identify a formal way to resolve the issue. For example: “I understand we cannot enter today. We will stop here and use the official process to rearrange the visit.” You can address any allegation or compensation question later through the proper procedure. If pushing, thrown objects, weapons or blocked exits appear, protecting the group becomes more important than finishing the conversation. ## 4.6 \| Refuse unsafe demands clearly A refusal can be safe and respectful. Somebody says the organiser is waiting in a private room, although the planned meeting was in a public lobby. If the arrangement remains voluntary, you can say: “Thank you. I will wait here until the organiser confirms the change.” A sudden request to enter an isolated place can be paused while you verify the arrangement. Use a known reception point or another verifiable arrangement. If the other person refuses, cancel the voluntary meeting. If force begins and your freedom is restricted, prioritise personal safety and reduce escalation. Avoid turning a disagreement into an armed struggle. Module 08 covers forced control and detention. ## 4.7 \| Interact with armed or official personnel At a temporary inspection point, language problems and uncertainty about the officers' authority can combine. Travellers may simultaneously search for documents, protest and begin filming. This can rapidly make the encounter less safe. Stop unnecessary movements, keep hands visible and let one person answer questions. Retrieve documents slowly when instructed. Request an interpreter where safe. If a permit is missing, ask about the formal process and follow an authorised process for resolving the restriction. If documents are confiscated or someone is taken to an unknown place, the event may have progressed beyond routine inspection. Preserve life first. The external tracing plan in Modules 05 and 10 is then relevant. ### Three levels of inspection demand different decisions At one end is an ordinary document check, after which the traveller can leave. A more restrictive procedure may require waiting in a designated area with an identifiable agency and process. At the serious end, documents and communications are taken away, the person is transferred, and no release procedure is explained. Calling all three situations “just cooperate with police” fails to explain the changing problem. Ask which authority or process applies when doing so is safe. If freedom has already been removed, protect yourself first and pursue legal assistance through the available channels. The companion who remains free should activate the missing-person process in Modules 05 and 10. ## 4.8 \| Know when to end a confrontation Ending an argument is itself a skill. When staff have clearly refused access and a crowd is gathering, repeating the same explanation may make it harder to leave safely. If the exit remains available, conclude briefly: “We will leave now and address this through the official channel.” Move away from the exposed entrance. If people are blocking movement, avoid shoving or provocative language and seek a safe opportunity to withdraw. A successful de-escalation may end with everyone leaving safely and resolving the permission issue later. Preventing injury and preserving a lawful way to resolve the issue later is a valuable outcome. Simulated training scene \| 4.8 Ending a high-risk confrontation and withdrawing safely. Observation: What shows that further explanation is increasing exposure? Safe action: Stop arguing when exits become obstructed or threats escalate; withdraw if safe, otherwise avoid sudden movements and seek protection. ### Worked scenario: an argument becomes detention A visitor argues that a ticket allows entry into a closed archaeological area. Staff refuse entry, armed personnel arrive, and the visitor's passport is retained. At first the dispute was about permission to enter. It has now become a question of control over a person. If you are the companion, stop trying to win the ticket argument. Establish who can still leave safely, which devices or documents were taken, and what direct evidence you can preserve from a safe place. The detained person and free companion have different responsibilities. The person being held prioritises life and health; the free companion begins a lawful search and identity-verification response. The course tests whether learners can distinguish those roles, and act within their own circumstances. ## Module-specific assessment Two visitors are asked to enter an unattended room to complete paperwork. Give a calm, realistic response that preserves a way to verify the request. Then explain when discussion of procedure must give way to personal protection because movement is restricted or weapons appear. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, use the explanations to find where your decisions were uncertain, then revisit the relevant course. modules.title: 05 | Movement and Vehicle Safety in High-Risk Areas
modules.body: Module 05 \| Movement and Vehicle Safety in High-Risk Areas In a hostile environment, a vehicle movement supports an operational task. Treat the movement as an activity with clear conditions, responsibilities and alternatives. Learn when movement is justified, how to protect passengers and when to stop or change the task. Learning outcome: Assess a necessary movement, identify unsafe transport, respond to checkpoints or interruptions and recognise the limits of non-specialist driving. ## 5.1 \| Set the purpose and limits of movement Plan the movement around the destination, exposure and available support. You may be travelling from a hotel to a historic site, attending a business meeting or visiting a remote facility. Check whether the destination, timing and actual protection still support the trip. A site may advertise that it is open while the surrounding roads remain subject to restrictions or violent incidents. Check what is actually permitted and what conditions would make you stop. Check access and safety conditions before proceeding. A necessary visit can sometimes be shortened, relocated or postponed without abandoning its underlying purpose. Your movement plan should give a trusted person outside the information and authority to act if you are detained or go missing. GOTWA is introduced below for that reason. ### GOTWA \| Make the final A an external response plan when someone disappears GOTWA is a short pre-movement handover: G for Going, O for Others, T for Time, W for What the receiver will do if overdue, and A for Actions each party will take if circumstances change. The final two points are essential for travel, sightseeing and short-term visits. If someone is moved into an undisclosed holding site, their phone may be confiscated. A route and an expected return time do not, by themselves, enable a search. Suppose two visitors enter a historic site. One is taken away by people claiming official authority. The companion sees where and when it happened but does not know the detaining agency. No public record or direct contact follows. The final A must tell the people outside how to act using the existing identity and last-location record. | Item | Practical information to agree before the activity | | --- | --- | | G — Going | Actual site, purpose, permissions and route; preserve the last location personally confirmed | | O — Others | Companions, legitimate organiser, guide or Fixer and their distinct roles | | T — Time | Expected return, known coverage gaps and circumstances requiring immediate escalation | | W — What | How to verify missed contact through companions, the venue and the original arrangements without treating rumours as facts | | A — Actions | Who submits identity and last-sighting evidence to the traveller's embassy or consulate; who engages a qualified lawyer and lawful local channels; how receipt and follow-up are recorded | An external receiver should be able to provide legal name, nationality, passport details through a secure channel, lawful entry or activity documentation, the last directly confirmed message and the witness account of being taken away. The receiver should explicitly identify what is unknown: which agency holds the person, where they were moved and whether a formal procedure exists. A local Fixer can verify arrangements, interpret accounts and support lawful contact with relevant offices. Formal legal and consular matters belong with qualified professionals. Keep any local enquiries lawful and record who was contacted. Where secret or arbitrary detention is suspected, legal and consular professionals must assess the appropriate next steps. A routine missed check-in can follow an agreed verification sequence. Eyewitness evidence of forcible removal, seizure of communications or immediate violence calls for urgent action without waiting for a scheduled check-in. Practice: Write a concise first report for a consular officer. Your companion's last message was at 14:12, and you saw the person taken from the site at 14:20. Distinguish what you witnessed from what remains unverified. ## 5.2 \| Check passengers and vehicles before departure Check the actual vehicle, driver and pickup arrangement. The person approaching you may know your name from a luggage tag or shared itinerary. Check unexpected changes to the driver, registration or pickup arrangement through an existing, reliable provider—not the phone number supplied by the stranger. Passengers can check conditions they can see. They should be able to see whether everyone has a working seat belt, whether doors and exits are usable, and whether luggage is secured. A driver or competent technician should check tyres, brakes, fuel and vehicle roadworthiness. Choose another vehicle if serious defects are visible. While you can still decline freely, stay in a legitimate staffed place to verify a changed pickup. If an armed person is already restricting your movements, insisting on a booking check may no longer be the safest priority. ### Passenger checks before departure Visitors can check essential passenger conditions: a separate seat and functional restraint for everyone, usable doors, secured luggage, and a driver who appears fit to drive. Serious tyre damage, overloading or fatigue call for a replacement vehicle or a delay. Passenger checks and professional vehicle inspection complement one another. Passengers can refuse a clearly unsafe vehicle; professional drivers and trained protection personnel handle specialist driving and convoy procedures. ## 5.3 \| Separate the roles of driver, escort and passenger In escorted travel, everyone should follow the assigned roles. The driver controls the vehicle; authorised security personnel manage protective decisions; passengers remain restrained, avoid interfering and follow their actual briefing. Everyone should know what is expected if vehicles become separated. Travellers arranging their own transport can manage several important risks: choose verified transport, comply with lawful restrictions, avoid unnecessary night movements and stop when the driver is exhausted. Keep professional driving and armed-protection manoeuvres with trained personnel. Gunfire, a roadblock or a collision may require different action. If an unknown obstacle blocks the road, pause and assess the situation from a protected position. Specialist manoeuvres require training and appropriate authority. ## 5.4 \| Avoid unnecessary exposure during movement Unnecessary exposure often happens during a short, casual stop. Passengers step out to photograph the road, gather behind the boot to discuss directions or stand outside a hotel entrance while waiting. Each action can place people into traffic, a crowd or an uncontrolled area while offering little practical benefit. Rest stops remain necessary, especially after long driving. Choose a location that can lawfully and safely be used, and consider whether people will be waiting in open exposure. A road acceptable in daylight may become restricted at night, which can turn an extra hour of sightseeing into a major change in risk. Suppose a remote visit ends two hours late. Ask whether the driver remains fit, the movement window is still valid, and a verified place can receive the group. Confirm the road before taking an unfamiliar detour. Simulated training scene \| 5.4 Temporary road closure conflicting with navigation (additional scenario). Observe: Officials redirect traffic while the navigation app still shows the original route open. Which information needs verification before moving? Act: Do not leave the vehicle to crowd or photograph the checkpoint, or improvise a route onto unknown tracks. From a safe position, the driver verifies official instructions, an approved alternative and communications; if safety cannot be confirmed, pause the journey and update the expected arrival time. Simulated training scene \| 5.4 Deciding whether to continue after an unscheduled stop. Observe: Does the stopping place increase exposure to traffic, crowds or heat? Are the vehicle, passengers and communications fit for continued movement? Act: Keep passengers in a confirmed safer position while the driver assesses the vehicle. Have the driver or a qualified technician assess the vehicle when safe, and use a reliable channel to report location, headcount and delay. Do not force onward travel before the conditions are verified. ### An unnecessary stop can create more exposure than the vehicle itself During travel through a region with frequent checks, a companion asks to stop for photographs, refreshments or filming officers. Once out of the vehicle, people may be exposed to passing traffic, crowds or unknown third parties. Stop at a lawful place with manageable traffic and security conditions. When a stop is unavoidable because of a breakdown or an authorised inspection, the safer place may be inside or outside depending on the actual hazards. Decide whether remaining inside or moving outside offers better immediate protection. ## 5.5 \| Respond to a blocked route or possible attack When the road ahead is closed, ask the driver what has happened. Check traffic directions, pedestrian access and conditions around the closure. Construction and ordinary accidents may leave a straightforward walking option. Unrest, gunfire or armed restrictions call for a safer destination away from the affected area. At a temporary barrier, observe lawful traffic management and avoid turning onto unfamiliar tracks to see whether they are passable. Passengers should not gather outside to investigate. If people are directly threatened or vehicles are forcibly controlled, the priority becomes protecting the passengers from immediate harm. If you decide to go back, choose a familiar place where the driver can stop safely and you can arrange your next move. A staffed hotel, shopping centre or fuel station may work, depending on local conditions. ### Road closure in a taxi: the meter is still running You are taking a taxi to a visitor site or business appointment. The road ahead closes, traffic stops and the fare keeps rising. Even the driver cannot say when the road will reopen. Option 1: If the walking route is safe, finish the taxi ride and walk. Ask the driver what caused the closure and how far you are from your destination. Check whether pedestrians are allowed through and the remaining walk is manageable. For ordinary roadworks or a traffic accident with an open footpath, have the driver stop at a permitted place, pay the current fare and continue on foot. Option 2: If walking is unsuitable, return to a safe place. If there is unrest, pedestrian access is closed, the distance is excessive or you are carrying heavy luggage, ask the driver to return to a known hotel, shopping centre or another location suitable for stopping and waiting. Settle the fare there, then rearrange transport or the visit. Practice: A driver says roadworks have blocked vehicles, but your destination is a ten-minute walk along an open pavement. What would you do? How would your decision change if the closure was caused by violent unrest? ### Choose your next step when the original route closes A familiar road is closed. The navigation app still shows a small side lane and the driver proposes trying it. Verify whether the road is open, legally usable and safe. The lane may enter a restricted military area, contaminated ground or a place with no safe turnaround. If your present location is not under direct threat, pause movement and verify official restrictions or legitimate diversion instructions. If violence is developing around you, protect people first. If the original route is no longer suitable, choose a safer plan and update the expected arrival. ## 5.6 \| Handle inspections and checkpoints A confrontational checkpoint is especially difficult when you do not speak the language. One person reaches for documents, another films, and several others argue about the law. Those combined actions can rapidly escalate tension. Stop filming. Keep your hands visible and make movements slowly. Explain before reaching for a passport, opening a bag or getting out, and follow instructions as safely as possible. Request interpretation when allowed. If documents are taken or movement is restricted, protecting life is more important than immediately winning an argument over property or procedure. At a tense inspection, keep movements clear and controlled. Once safe, address legal concerns through professional or consular channels. If somebody is taken away without an identified destination, Modules 08 and 10 explain the detainee's and external receiver's separate actions. Simulated training scene \| 5.6 Checkpoint document inspection. Observe: Which sudden movements could be misinterpreted when documents or equipment are requested? What facts need checking if a document is retained? Act: Stop filming, keep hands visible and explain before reaching for items. Use one calm spokesperson; do not grab documents back or drive away without authorisation. Seek assistance through an appropriate channel when safe. ## 5.7 \| Manage breakdowns and collision hazards A vehicle breakdown can create several dangers at once. On a narrow road, passing vehicles may be the most immediate threat. In a hot and isolated area, exposure and lack of water may become significant. In a violent area, an unnecessarily prolonged roadside gathering may increase vulnerability. The driver should stop safely and arrange appropriate warning measures within local rules. Passengers should avoid gathering in a traffic lane or another exposed position and check for injuries. Mechanical repair belongs to competent people. Where mobile service is absent, a tested lawful backup can support a rescue request; do not send companions roaming into unfamiliar terrain to find a signal. An active fire or attack may require leaving the vehicle. A manageable mechanical fault in a dangerous outside environment may require a different decision. Identify the immediate hazard before acting. ### After a breakdown, prevent a second collision A vehicle stops on a narrow road. Passengers gather behind it to discuss a tyre. That may place them in the path of following traffic. First consider approaching vehicles, fire hazards and local security before deciding where passengers can wait. The trained driver should handle lawful warning measures and mechanical arrangements. Ask the driver to check the repaired vehicle before continuing. Recheck the problem, the driver and the passengers before resuming. ## 5.8 \| Stop, return or resume a movement A movement is complete when everyone has safely reached a place able to receive them—not when the driver says they are nearly there. A delayed visit, unexpected road closure or an unwell companion can change what was safe a few hours earlier. Before resuming movement, reconsider the passengers, the driver and vehicle, the direct danger in the environment, and the receiving location. An evening deadline or the feeling that 'we have already come this far' does not make missing safety conditions reappear. GOTWA also matters when a traveller is taken from an inspection point or historical site. The others should protect themselves, preserve the last facts they witnessed and allow the agreed external Action plan to begin without relying on the missing person's device. Simulated training scene \| 5.8 Deciding whether movement can resume after a road closure. Observe: Is the route still controlled, are the occupants and vehicle fit to move, and can the receiving location accept them? Act: Do not force passage or gather outside the vehicle. Verify an approved alternative, reception arrangements and personnel status from a safe position; suspend movement and update the journey plan if conditions remain unconfirmed. Simulated training scene \| 5.8 Vehicle and occupant readiness before resuming a journey (supporting exercise). Observe: The bonnet is open and people are waiting beside the vehicle while contacting others. Does this prove the fault has been resolved or the driver is fit to continue? What must be verified separately? Act: Keep passengers in a position protected from traffic and local threats. Have a qualified person assess the fault and roadworthiness; confirm driver fitness, passenger accountability and a fallback vehicle. Do not restart merely because the road has reopened or the schedule is pressing. ## Module-specific assessment A vehicle is stopped by restrictions. Navigation suggests an unfamiliar track and a passenger has a defective seat belt. Assess road access, vehicle condition and personnel safety separately. Explain what conditions must be checked before the journey can continue. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, read the explanations and revisit the specific skill behind each missed question. modules.title: 06 | Accommodation, Public Venues and Site Protection
modules.body: Module 06 \| Accommodation, Public Venues and Site Protection The protection offered by a venue depends on its entrances, exits, staff and response arrangements. Learn to recognise gaps in access control and take suitable action during intrusion, alarms, outages, fire and violence outside a compound. Learning outcome: Identify exposure at a workplace, follow access controls and select protective or evacuation actions according to the danger. ## 6.1 \| Recognise threats around a facility When entering a hotel, exhibition venue or industrial site, identify the protection the place actually offers. Each setting has different access controls, fire precautions and protective features. Early on, identify who can enter, where you can leave in a fire and which parts of the building could reduce exposure to violence outside. A hotel may have a staffed front desk but an unsecured service entrance. A museum may have a barrier yet allow uncontrolled access from parking. A construction site may leave a side gate open during deliveries. Each weakness affects a different part of the site's protection. Visitors can carry out a short practical check. They should recognise obvious defects, understand the immediate effect on their safety and be willing to change rooms, venues or activities when protection is inadequate. ## 6.2 \| Follow access and visitor controls A visitor's identity and purpose need to be checked in hotels as well as industrial sites. Someone knocking at your room may claim to be maintenance staff and know your room number. Confirm the visitor's identity through the hotel's established contact channel. Use the hotel's known front-desk channel to confirm an unexpected visit before opening the door. At a conference or historic site, do not follow an unidentified person into a restricted area simply because they claim to know the organiser. Worksite visitors should not be admitted using another person's access pass. Forced entry or weapons create an immediate security threat. Move away from direct danger and use the available protection. ### Checking an unexpected hotel visitor At 10 p.m., someone knocks and correctly states your name and room number. They claim to be a maintenance worker and demand immediate access. Those details might come from a legitimate work order, or from luggage labels, booking records or overheard conversation. The meaningful check is to contact the hotel through a channel you already know and ask whether maintenance was assigned, by whom and for what reason. If the lock is being forced or the person makes direct threats, the problem is no longer routine identity checking. Move away from the immediate exposure, use a protective option that is actually available, and seek help through building or emergency services. ## 6.3 \| Know safe internal areas and exits People often remember the door through which they entered but forget other exits. In a fire, that can send everyone back towards an overcrowded lobby. When you enter accommodation or a public venue, identify a usable stairway, the exit direction and the nearest staffed point. There is no universal “safest floor”. Distance to stairs, mobility limitations, exposure from windows, building construction and fire systems all affect the choice. Never block a fire exit with luggage or furniture. A shooting outside and smoke inside require different responses. The first may justify staying away from external windows in a protected internal area. The second may require evacuation under fire guidance. Follow the instructions for the danger actually affecting the building. Simulated training scene \| 6.3 Protected areas and exits. Observation: Does a blocked exit call for the same response during a fire and gunfire outside? Safe action: Identify a usable alternate route and protected interior location in advance; evacuate or shelter according to the actual threat and choose a protected position or safe evacuation route as appropriate. ### Similar alarms can require opposite actions | Current danger | Unsafe blanket rule | Relevant consideration | | --- | --- | --- | | Smoke and fire inside | Always lock the door and wait | Use fire procedures and assess whether a safe exit exists | | Gunfire outside | Always gather at the main gate | Compare internal structural protection against exposed movement | | Violence at an entrance | Always leave by the familiar door | Is that exit actually usable without entering the threat? | | Power outage without smoke | Run down a dark stairwell | Check emergency lighting, stairs and other immediate hazards | The best protective location depends on the threat. It has to remain protective against the threat now present. ## 6.4 \| Protect credentials and sensitive site information Passport details, hotel room numbers, visitor badges and photographs of a technical site can expose more information than expected. Legitimate identity checks are necessary, but keep travel patterns and restricted-site details out of public posts. Before posting a photograph, inspect the background for a room number, access pass, sensitive control system or location that reveals where colleagues are staying. Delay public posts where necessary and use appropriate device access controls. Check links and account access carefully, and follow local communications laws. If a phone is seized or lost, an independent protected identity backup becomes more important than the settings on that phone. ## 6.5 \| Notice protective failures during routine work Facilities can lose protection through everyday failures: blocked emergency stairs, a delivery door left open, failed lighting or a temporarily closed museum exit. These conditions weaken the protection available during an emergency. A hotel guest can report a blocked escape route and request another room or consider leaving an unsafe section. A visiting technician should report failed site controls through the established procedure. Neither should experiment with electrical boards or dangerous infrastructure. The practical skill is recognising which capability has failed, what harm could result and whether your activity can safely continue until that capability is restored. ## 6.6 \| Respond to outages, fire and building failures A power failure affects more than comfort. Electronic door controls, lifts, corridors, emergency lighting and some communications may stop working. In a high-rise hotel, this can change the safety of an exit; at an industrial site it may also create uncontrolled equipment hazards. Check for smoke, electrical danger and actual lighting. Use suitable battery-powered lights. Do not light open flames or tamper with unfamiliar electrical equipment. Follow the building's emergency instructions and avoid entering affected technical areas. When fire, smoke or a dangerous building failure develops, the decision changes from routine temporary inconvenience to immediate safety action. ## 6.7 \| Take cover during gunfire or attempted intrusion When gunfire or unrest develops outside accommodation, many people move to windows or the entrance to find out what is happening. Those positions may increase exposure. Move away from obvious external openings and use suitable internal protection if available. A safe haven is an actual location that is open, accessible and able to offer temporary protection. It might be a suitably managed hotel or agreed facility. Check with the embassy or other receiving facility before travelling there for shelter; follow lawful access procedures. Keep checking whether the building remains protective. If smoke, fire or intrusion makes the building unsafe, reassess. Wait for reliable information before moving into exposed areas. ### An armed attack in a public venue Shots are heard inside an exhibition building. Some visitors follow a crowd towards a glass entrance; another notices a room with a door that can be secured. Check where the attacker is, what lies along the exit route and whether the internal room provides useful protection. Leave along a clearly safe direction where possible. If that is not available, use a feasible internal shelter when the exit is under threat. Do not treat a lift as an all-purpose escape option. Do not return to a threatened room for passports, laptops or luggage. ## 6.8 \| Account for people and verify before restarting work After an alert, check essential access, fire safety and personnel accountability before resuming. Access controls may be damaged, emergency exits blocked, equipment affected or someone still unaccounted for. Before a visit or work activity resumes, confirm the people involved and the protective functions necessary for that activity. A traveller can choose to leave or change plans when essential protection is unavailable. Confirm each person directly through a reliable channel. A missing or detained person requires a separate, continuing tracing process. Simulated training scene \| 6.8 Image 1: Personnel accountability (first image below). Observation: Whose status or location remains unconfirmed after an alert? Safe action: Account for each person using the roster, follow the missing-person procedure, and do not resume operations merely because the area is quiet. Simulated training scene \| 6.8 Image 2: Conditions for restarting work (second image above). Observation: Does accounting for personnel prove the facility is safe to use? Safe action: Check damaged locks, power, exits and equipment; restrict unverified areas until competent checks and authorised approval are complete. ### Checking conditions before staying after an alert After unrest outside, the front desk resumes check-ins. Yet a fire exit remains blocked, access control has been damaged, and one companion has not been accounted for. A guest can decide to change rooms, leave or suspend activities based on the conditions now available. Check usable exits, room security, fire protection, reliable communications and the actual whereabouts of companions. Consider changing rooms, suspending the activity or relocating to a genuinely available place when that is safer. Check the exits, access control, communications and security conditions yourself. ## Module-specific assessment A hotel's entrance is affected by violent unrest, but its interior is initially usable. Smoke then enters a stairwell. Explain why a previously sensible decision to shelter may become unsafe. Identify what would make a protective location or exit genuinely usable. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, use the explanations to find where your decisions were uncertain, then revisit the relevant course.
