modules.title: 07 | Armed Violence, Civil Unrest and Explosive Hazards
modules.body: Module 07 \| Armed Violence, Civil Unrest and Explosive Hazards Gunfire, riots, explosions and suspicious items demand different immediate responses. Learn to reduce exposure, use genuine protection, avoid explosive hazards and revise your decision when the situation changes. Learning outcome: Recognise the type of danger and take the first protective action without approaching, filming or attempting to clear hazards. ## 7.1 \| Recognise when unrest is escalating At a public gathering, watch how people and security forces behave, and whether exits remain open. What matters to a visitor is whether conditions are changing: objects are being thrown, police and crowds are clashing, shops are closing, exits are blocked or weapons and fire are present. Imagine visiting a museum beside a square where a demonstration is growing. At first, there may be no reason to approach the crowd. Check whether the museum remains a viable place to wait and whether staff know which exits can be used. If people begin forcing the entrance, move visitors away from the exposed perimeter. For personal safety, check whether violence is approaching and where you can find practical protection. Simulated training scene \| 7.1 Crowd disruption of pickup and site access. Observe: Has the crowd blocked the gate, and can the planned vehicle still approach safely? Action: Suspend movement through the affected entrance; do not send anyone into the crowd to find transport. Account for personnel from a protected location and confirm an alternative pickup only when safe. Simulated training scene \| 7.1 Crowd activity at the site boundary. Observe: What signals suggest escalation, and which access route may become unusable? Action: Stop nonessential work near the perimeter and withdraw to a controlled area; do not use an exposed gate until its safety is confirmed. ### The danger may be outside the centre of a demonstration A visitor is taking photographs in a public square. Nearby shops begin lowering shutters and police restrict access to a side street. The crowd remains peaceful, but walking towards the restriction to ask questions may take the visitor from a normal public space into an area of confrontation. Pause photography, stay out of the contact area and determine whether the current venue remains safe. At a peaceful gathering, maintain distance and monitor access routes. Thrown objects, chemical irritants, blocked exits or armed threats mean the exposure has changed. The learner should name a concrete condition that would end the visit, using changes they can actually observe. ## 7.2 \| Avoid exposure to clashes and crowds Moving between a crowd and a police line can expose a person to pushing, thrown objects, chemical irritants or armed violence. A gap visible from a doorway may close as the crowd changes direction. Suppose a visiting team cannot reach its pickup vehicle because streets are full of demonstrators. One companion has an injured ankle. Do not drag the person through the confrontation or leave them behind. Assess whether the current venue remains usable and whether there is a genuinely open alternative exit or professional assistance. If smoke or violence enters the building, sheltering conditions change. Reassess the shelter and any usable exit whenever the danger changes. Simulated training scene \| 7.2 A second view of escalating unrest. Observe: How do smoke, crowd movement and blocked routes change the safest option? Action: Do not cross opposing groups or move toward smoke and fire. Withdraw by a known safe route, or shelter in a protective location and request assistance when the route is uncertain. ## 7.3 \| Respond to gunfire nearby When shots are heard, stop exposed activity and move towards genuine protection. Move away from windows, doors and open spaces. Use substantial structural protection where available and avoid going towards the sound to record what is happening. Running towards the hotel may sound sensible, but it could also mean crossing an exposed area in the direction of gunfire. If a usable protected area is nearby, it may be the better immediate option. Wait for reliable confirmation that an exit route can be used. Keep slower or injured companions with the group and choose a route that everyone can use safely. Simulated training scene \| 7.3 Armed threat in an urban street. Observe: Which positions are exposed, and which objects may provide concealment without reliable ballistic protection? Action: Move away from windows and open ground; use substantial structural protection where possible. Do not approach to identify or film the armed person. ### Assessing exposure when gunfire is heard Buildings can reflect gunshots. An untrained person may be unable to tell their direction or distance reliably. Echoes between buildings can distort the perceived distance and direction of gunfire. In an open historic site, minimise exposure and seek whatever genuine protection is accessible. Already inside a substantial building, compare staying protected with any exposed route to another location. Check what is happening beyond an exit before moving. The choice also changes when a group includes a child, older person or companion who cannot move quickly. ## 7.4 \| Understand concealment versus cover Concealment hides a person from view; cover provides physical protection. Curtains, lightweight furniture and ordinary vehicle doors can hide a person from view without reliably stopping projectiles or fragments. Substantial structures may offer better protection, but assess the actual structure and available alternatives. Moving from a relatively protected room through a long glass lobby may increase exposure even when the lobby is the familiar way out. Compare the danger along the movement route with the protection currently available. Focus on reducing exposure using the available building structure. Avoid assuming that a position is bulletproof merely because it looks solid. ## 7.5 \| Respond to the aftermath of an explosion An explosion can leave shattered glass, smoke, falling objects, damaged structures and casualties. Running towards the blast site to investigate may expose rescuers to continuing hazards. First check whether you and your companions are in ongoing danger. After a blast near a hotel, move away from broken windows and obvious structural damage. Check for smoke and fire inside. If the building remains usable and the street is uncertain, do not go outside simply to identify the cause. If smoke spreads within the building, follow an appropriate emergency exit procedure. Aid for casualties begins when approaching them is reasonably safe. Module 09 explains the medical priorities once the rescuer is no longer adding to the incident. ### The second decision after a blast: can you reach casualties safely? Seeing an injured person near a blast creates an urge to run in immediately. But fire, smoke, falling material, damaged power supplies and unknown hazardous items may still be present. Where continuing attack is possible, an unplanned approach can create more casualties. First identify what threatens people from your current position, call appropriate responders, and help only where reasonably safe and within your training. Once safe, report what you actually observed: time of blast, visible damage, estimated casualties and any continuing danger. Do not go back for a better photograph. ## 7.6 \| Recognise mines and unexploded ordnance Conflict-affected areas may contain mines and unexploded ordnance long after fighting has stopped. Visitors exploring old buildings or taking photographs off marked paths can be especially vulnerable because the danger may not look like an obvious explosive device. Warning signs, disturbed ground, abandoned ammunition and routes that others avoid are reasons to stop approaching. Stay on designated and verified routes. Do not touch, dig, move or attempt to identify a suspicious object at close range. Withdraw by a route already known to be safer and leave assessment to qualified explosive-ordnance specialists. Never send an untrained companion ahead to test the ground. ## 7.7 \| Withdraw from a suspected device A suspicious package or unusual item may have an innocent explanation. But attempting to open, move or photograph it at close range merely to resolve uncertainty can create unnecessary danger. At a hotel, historic site or work location, stop approaching the item and discourage others from gathering around it. Withdraw using an appropriate known route, and describe where it was seen to competent personnel from a safer location. Keep away from suspicious objects and notify trained authorities from a safe position. Simulated training scene \| 7.7 Suspected roadside hazard. Observe: What can be seen from an already safe position, and which verge or ground areas remain unverified? Action: Do not approach, touch, move or dismantle the object, or enter an unverified verge. Prevent others from approaching, withdraw by a known safe route and report from safety for specialist response. ## 7.8 \| Act during a direct armed attack During a direct armed attack, the right immediate action depends on the attacker, the usable exits and the protection available. If a clearly safer exit leads away from the attacker, leave without approaching the threat. If escape is not feasible, use a space that limits access and provides the best realistic protection. Use an exit only if it leads safely away from the attacker. Fire or smoke may also change whether sheltering remains possible. In an extreme situation of imminent lethal harm with no safe alternative, last-resort self-protection may be necessary. Prioritise escape or practical shelter before any last-resort self-protection. ### Checkpoints and direct armed attacks require different responses At a checkpoint, watch the officials' instructions; during a direct attack, focus on escaping or reaching protection. At a checkpoint, sudden flight or attempts to force passage may escalate a misunderstanding. During a direct attack, a clearly safe exit away from the attacker may instead require immediate use. The first situation calls for controlled movements and clarification when possible; the second for reducing exposure to lethal violence. Judge the immediate danger from the armed person's actions. If no safe escape route exists during an attack, consider a genuinely protective internal position and avoid the entrance under attack. ## Module-specific assessment Compare the first protective action in three events: objects thrown during a demonstration, gunfire of uncertain direction and suspected unexploded ordnance. Explain why a response appropriate to one hazard must not be copied blindly to another. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, use the explanations to find where your decisions were uncertain, then revisit the relevant course. modules.title: 08 | Kidnapping Prevention, Detention, and Survival
modules.body: Module 08 \| Kidnapping, Detention and Coercion Criminal abduction, violent robbery and lawful detention are different situations. Learn to notice attempted isolation, protect life when controlled, request lawful help and recover after release. Learning outcome: Recognise forced-control indicators and avoid escalating an immediate threat while preserving health and access to appropriate support. ## 8.1 \| Distinguish abduction, robbery and detention Losing freedom of movement abroad can mean several different things: a routine check, formal arrest, detention without a clear legal process, or abduction by criminals. To a companion, these may initially look the same: somebody has been taken away and will not answer a phone. Record what witnesses saw, then use legal, consular and local channels to identify the agency and location. Imagine a visitor taken from a historic site by people who identify themselves as officials. The witness sees a vehicle depart but cannot identify the authority or a place of detention. The witness should record the time, location, what the officials said and the last directly verified message. Those facts allow consular and legal assistance to begin. For the person being taken away, the immediate priority is survival and avoiding unnecessary confrontation. For the person outside, the priority is accurate reporting and lawful tracing. These are two different responses. Simulated training scene \| 8.1 Recognising forced removal from a safe area. Observe: Is someone being compelled to leave the normal work area, enter an unidentified vehicle or separate from colleagues? Can the person's authority and lawful process be verified? Act: When safe to decline, avoid isolated locations and verify through a trusted channel. Under immediate violent threat, prioritise life and avoid dangerous resistance. ### Tracing someone taken into unknown custody People in uniform take someone from a heritage site. This might involve lawful checking, an identification problem, custody without due process, or a criminal group impersonating officials. Witnesses often know only who took the person, where and when. The status of the custody still needs to be established through competent channels. Reports must separate directly observed facts from conclusions that cannot yet be supported. The person being taken should focus on personal safety; outside helpers should continue lawful enquiries even if no public custody record is available. Give the witness, receiver and detained person distinct tasks. ## 8.2 \| Reduce the chance of being targeted Keeping a low profile means limiting unnecessary exposure of your movements while meeting normal legal identity requirements. Travellers leave fragments of information in hotel bookings, luggage tags, visitor records, social media and photographs. Put together, these details can disclose where a person sleeps, what they do and when they will be alone. Do not post your next location in real time or distribute a complete itinerary to everyone in a group chat. Yet a trusted external person should hold enough identifying and travel information to support a lawful search if you are taken away. Give a trusted external receiver the information needed for tracing in an emergency. Before visiting an unfamiliar high-risk location, make sure an agreed external receiver can identify your legal name, nationality, permitted activities, travelling companions and last planned location using the backup arranged before departure. ## 8.3 \| Recognise isolation and lure attempts An attempt to isolate a traveller may sound quite ordinary: “The organiser is upstairs”, “The entrance has moved”, or “You must come to a private office alone”. These explanations may be genuine. What matters is whether the proposed change can be verified and whether you still have a real choice. Suppose two visitors expect to meet in a public reception area. Someone insists that one visitor follow them into a private room, cannot give the organiser's name and refuses the presence of a companion. While departure is still voluntary, stay in a staffed area and confirm the arrangement through an established channel. A simple request to confirm the meeting with the organiser is enough to pause the encounter. If an exit is blocked, weapons appear or force is used, the circumstances have changed. The right response now focuses on reducing harm while avoiding movements that could escalate a direct physical threat. ## 8.4 \| Respond to violent robbery or threats An armed robber may demand a phone, passport, wallet or work equipment. The instinct to protect important documents can be strong, especially when losing a passport would prevent onward travel. During a direct armed threat, protect life first and deal with property afterward. Keep movements slow and visible as far as circumstances permit. If you need to take something from a pocket, explain the movement when safe and possible. Do not try to seize a weapon or chase the assailant. Keep movements predictable and adapt to the person's instructions and behaviour. After reaching safety, deal with injuries, identity documents, financial accounts and official reporting. A lawful backup copy of identification, medicine information and emergency contacts can reduce the consequences of losing a bag or phone, but it is never worth a violent struggle. Simulated training scene \| 8.4 Armed robbery. Observe: Armed people are controlling a worker and searching property beside an SUV. Which movements could be mistaken for resistance, and what safe exits cannot be established from the image alone? Act: Prioritise life over property, keep hands and movements visible, explain slowly before reaching for an item, and avoid sudden gestures. Report and assess injuries once safely away. ## 8.5 \| Survive the first stage of forced control The first stage of forced confinement can be frightening because almost everything is uncertain. You may not know where you are being taken or whether the people outside know what happened. Breathing steadily, keeping your hands and movements predictable, and listening for simple instructions can help you avoid adding danger. When it is safe to ask, keep essential requests short and consistent: water, food, a toilet, necessary medication, medical attention, an interpreter or notification of your embassy. Do not invent an identity or make complicated claims about legal matters you do not understand. Record dates or names only if permitted and doing so will not increase danger. Any chance to leave detention must be assessed against the immediate danger. Do not organise confrontation or attempt dangerous resistance merely because the first effort to contact the outside world has failed. Focus on food, water, medication, hygiene and safe opportunities for formal assistance. Simulated training scene \| 8.5 Initial period under forced control. Observe: Which movements are restricted, and is there an urgent injury, medication need or breathing difficulty? Act: Prioritise life, keep movements slow and visible, and state essential medical needs when safe. Avoid sudden resistance or escape attempts without a viable safe route. ### The first hour of forced control: maintaining basic safety When ordered to sit, wait or enter a vehicle, the individual may have no idea what follows. Keep movements measured and avoid sudden reaching for a phone, passport or paper card in a hidden clothing pocket. If it can be done safely, communicate an urgent need for interpretation, medication or medical care. The urge to “try one bold move” can be powerful. There is no general escape tactic that can safely be taught for every detention or captivity setting. Reducing immediate injury risk, keeping your identity clear and preserving basic health are meaningful actions under extreme loss of control. ## 8.6 \| Protect yourself during official detention A traveller may be held without a formal charge, interview or clear procedure. In conflict-affected or weakly governed areas, the expected institutions may not operate as they should. Extended custody without a clear procedure requires preparation for prolonged confinement and persistent external tracing. When safe, state your true identity and nationality, ask what authority is holding you and why, request a qualified interpreter and lawyer, and ask for your embassy or consulate to be notified. Communicate urgent medical needs plainly. Such requests may be delayed or refused; access may require persistent support from legal and consular representatives or release. Avoid guessing the meaning of documents you cannot read. Seek translation or legal assistance where possible, while protecting yourself if coercion escalates. Meanwhile, people outside should start lawful enquiries based on confirmed identity and the last verified location, using the last direct evidence and the agreed external action plan. Simulated training scene \| 8.6 Communicating while freedom is restricted. Observe: Can the image alone establish whether this is lawful detention or criminal coercion? Have identity, grounds and process been explained? Act: Avoid sudden movements and escalation. When safe, request qualified interpretation, legal or consular support and communicate urgent medical needs; do not substitute improvised resistance for lawful assistance. ## 8.7 \| Maintain health during prolonged captivity Weeks of confinement create problems beyond the first shock: disturbed sleep, uncertain dates, poor hygiene, irregular food and medication, deteriorating health and anxiety about being forgotten. The goal becomes maintaining physical and mental function one day at a time. Drink and eat when you can, maintain basic cleanliness and rest, and use light movement when permitted. Explain serious symptoms and essential medication requirements calmly and specifically. Avoid consuming unknown medicines simply to secure a promise. If a reliable legal, consular or independent visitor becomes available, explain your health needs and treatment accurately. Try not to interpret silence from outside as proof that nobody is looking. Keep important dates or events in mind if safe to do so, but do not risk punishment merely to maintain a secret record. Wait for actual release arrangements to be carried out. Preserving health and taking safe opportunities to request assistance are the immediate priorities. ### Maintaining a routine during prolonged detention Uncertainty over weeks can damage sleep, appetite, attention and time perception. Where conditions allow, build a small routine around meals, water, hygiene, rest and gentle movement. If dates cannot be established, use meals, rest and any available light cycle to maintain a routine. Retain useful memories of transfers and significant events when this can be done without provoking further danger. Be specific about illness, dehydration and essential medication: “I need drinking water”, “I need this medicine regularly”, or “I have chest pain and need a doctor.” Practise the relevant phrases before travel. Requests may need to be repeated at safer opportunities, without turning frustration into harmful confrontation. ## 8.8 \| Recover and reassess after release After release, address the person's safety, health and legal needs. A person held for weeks may be exhausted, malnourished, medically unwell or distressed. Begin with a genuinely safe reception location, identity verification, urgent health needs, privacy and practical support—not interviews or an immediate return to the original trip. Recounting detention repeatedly can be distressing. Lawyers, clinicians and other suitable professionals can arrange factual records and follow-up when the person is ready. Their needs should determine the pace. Public photographs or accounts should not be posted without consent. A later review should ask whether witnesses preserved the last confirmed location, whether an external receiver held identity documentation, and whether consular, legal and local tracing channels had accurate information. The objective is to shorten the next period of uncertainty, not blame a person for failing to escape. Simulated training scene \| 8.8 Safety and health after release. Observe: Can the image alone establish that the person is safe, medically stable or ready to resume work? Act: Arrange a safe location and appropriate medical assessment first, protect privacy, notify family appropriately and offer follow-up support. Do not demand repeated accounts or treat release as clearance for duty. ### After release, address health, identity documents and travel permission Identity may be verified and release approved while travel documents, immigration records or health remain unresolved. First reach a genuinely safe reception location, restore appropriate communication with trusted people, and seek medical assessment. Qualified legal assistance can then address identification, travel permission and documented facts. Someone deprived of liberty for two months needs time for health assessment, basic recovery and any formal travel procedures or face repeated interviews simply because they are out of the holding facility. ## Module-specific assessment A tourist is taken away at a heritage site and cannot be contacted for weeks. Identify the separate roles of the last witness, the external receiver and the detained person. Address identity verification, essential health needs, lawful enquiries and which health and administrative steps are needed before travel resumes. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, use the explanations to find where your decisions were uncertain, then revisit the relevant course. [Open quiz.ravenlong.com online quiz \| 15 questions →](https://quiz.ravenlong.com/en/08/)

modules.title: 09 | Emergency Medical Action and Stress in Hostile Environments
modules.body: Module 09 \| Emergency Medical Action and Stress in Hostile Environments When someone is injured, survival depends on avoiding further danger, recognising urgent problems and getting appropriate help. This module explains what non-specialists can do and what requires practical training. Learning outcome: Protect yourself and casualties, recognise medical emergencies and deliver a useful handover to responders. ## 9.1 \| Check scene safety before providing aid When someone is injured, the instinct to rush towards them is understandable. In a hostile environment, however, the casualty may still be exposed to gunfire, moving traffic, falling debris or electrical hazards. Creating another casualty can make rescue much harder. First decide whether you can safely approach. If direct violence continues, request competent assistance from a safer position and avoid entering the danger without appropriate protection and training. As conditions improve, give the help that is within your ability. At a roadside collision, for example, traffic may be a more immediate hazard to rescuers than the injury itself. Protecting yourself is part of keeping the rescue possible. Simulated training scene \| 9.1 Secondary hazards before casualty access. Observe: Are electrical hazards, moving traffic or continuing violence present along the approach? Act: Do not touch suspected live equipment or enter an unverified area; request professional help from safety and report the casualty's location and observable hazards. ## 9.2 \| Identify immediately life-threatening changes Non-specialists should not spend the first minutes debating a diagnosis. Check whether a casualty responds, breathes normally and has obvious major external bleeding. These observations help identify immediate life threats. After making sure the scene can be approached, seek emergency medical services promptly. If someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, follow applicable CPR and AED guidance from your training or emergency dispatcher. Major bleeding also demands urgent attention, with interventions appropriate to your training. A casualty who can still talk may nevertheless be seriously injured. Worsening consciousness, abnormal breathing or significant bleeding requires urgent professional care. ### How an untrained companion can be useful A visitor collapses in a hotel lobby. One person checks responsiveness, another holds a phone, and several bystanders crowd around asking whether it is heat exhaustion. Effective help depends on clear roles, not everyone guessing a diagnosis. One person should call local emergency services and follow the dispatcher. Someone with appropriate training checks breathing and serious bleeding. Others can bring an AED or first-aid kit, guide responders into the building and keep space around the casualty. If the person is not breathing normally, urgent action under applicable first-aid guidance cannot wait for a diagnosis. The approach changes again if fire, violence or another immediate danger threatens rescuers. ## 9.3 \| Give first aid within your competence A first-aid kit, automated external defibrillator or bleeding-control equipment is not useful merely because it is present. Before entering a remote setting, know where essential equipment is and whether anyone has actually been trained to use it. Without advanced training you can still contribute: call emergency services, give an accurate location and access point, bring the necessary kit, follow dispatcher instructions and keep the area safe for responders. Do not crowd the casualty or attempt invasive procedures after watching a brief video. Good emergency participation means carrying out the tasks you can safely perform and allowing competent responders to handle specialist care. ## 9.4 \| Act on severe external bleeding Severe external bleeding is time critical. If you can approach safely, seek urgent medical support and follow appropriate first-aid or dispatcher guidance for direct pressure and other bleeding-control measures. Use suitable protection from blood exposure where available. Learn tourniquet use and wound packing through supervised practical training. In an emergency, use the first aid you are trained to provide and follow dispatcher instructions. At the same time, an ongoing armed threat, fire or moving traffic may force a different immediate protection decision. Start urgent care and obtain medical help before dealing with photographs, insurance or responsibility. Simulated training scene \| 9.4 Severe external bleeding. Observe: Is the scene still dangerous, and are there signs of major bleeding or abnormal responsiveness or breathing? Act: Call emergency services, assist within your training and dispatcher guidance, and leave complex interventions to trained responders. ### Recognising serious bleeding A small graze may allow time for ordinary first aid. Clothing rapidly becoming soaked with blood, persistent major bleeding and deterioration in the casualty's condition point to a potentially life-threatening emergency. Seek urgent medical help. Where it is safe to approach, use direct pressure within your training and dispatcher guidance. Do not delay assistance to take photographs or debate how the injury happened. Tourniquets, wound packing and CPR require supervised hands-on practice for reliable performance. Build practical competence through supervised training. ## 9.5 \| Recognise breathing problems and serious trauma After an injury, watch for changes in consciousness, breathing and circulation. After a blast or serious collision, someone without obvious wounds may become pale, short of breath, confused or increasingly drowsy. Deterioration after an accident requires urgent medical assessment. While awaiting help, monitor responsiveness, breathing and visible bleeding. Avoid unnecessary movement unless the immediate environment makes staying more dangerous, and follow medical guidance on positioning. Tell responders how the injury happened and when symptoms changed. Confirm the receiving clinic's actual capability. A receiving facility's actual capability matters. ## 9.6 \| Respond to heat, cold and prolonged exposure Heat, cold, dehydration and prolonged exposure can turn routine sightseeing or field visits into medical emergencies. Confusion, altered behaviour or collapse during extreme heat may indicate a serious heat illness. Stop activity, move to a cooler place when safe, seek urgent medical assistance and begin appropriate cooling as directed. Cold exposure requires protection from wind and wet clothing and suitable warming. Protect the person from wind and wet clothing and seek suitable warming and medical care. Persistent vomiting, diarrhoea or inability to obtain safe water can create serious dehydration. The essential decision is knowing when water and a short rest are no longer an adequate response and the activity must stop. Simulated training scene \| 9.6 Heat-related illness. Observe: Is the person confused, unusually slow to respond or unable to work safely? Act: Stop heat exposure, move to a safer cooler area and seek emergency care for suspected heatstroke; begin safe cooling as directed and arrange urgent care before any return to normal activity. ### Confusion and serious illness during heat exposure During a hot-weather visit, a companion develops a headache, then begins walking unsteadily and answers questions incoherently. Keep the person accompanied, stop the activity and seek urgent medical help. Confusion may indicate a serious heat illness or another medical emergency. Stop exposure, seek urgent medical care and cool the person safely under professional guidance. Cold exposure presents different dangers: wet clothing, prolonged wind and a declining level of responsiveness can signal hypothermia. No single instruction to “drink water and rest” covers every environmental illness. ## 9.7 \| Support people after a traumatic event After violence, detention or an explosion, one person may be silent while another talks repeatedly. Provide calm support, rest, water and clear information about what happens next. Begin by removing ongoing danger and meeting basic needs such as rest, water, food and reliable information. Do not force a newly released detainee to recount weeks of confinement or participate in interviews. Ask what they need now, listen if they wish to speak, and avoid posting images or personal details without permission. Severe ongoing distress, loss of normal functioning or risk of self-harm requires professional mental-health or medical support. People recovering from prolonged confinement may need ongoing medical and psychological support. ## 9.8 \| Arrange a medical transfer and handover Medical transfer means more than finding a vehicle. The appropriate transport, care during movement, actual ability of a hospital to receive a casualty and the safe route all matter. A nearby clinic in an unstable area may be unable to manage major trauma. Give responders a concise handover: exact location, number of casualties, time and mechanism of injury, responsiveness, breathing, severe bleeding and assistance already provided. Relevant medication or allergy details should be shared with professionals as needed, through a private medical handover. For sudden severe chest pain, call emergency medical services immediately and deal with insurance afterward. Follow local emergency medical advice to obtain appropriate care and transfer. Simulated training scene \| 9.8 Medical transfer and handover. Observe: Which facts about the casualty, departure time, receiving facility and en-route support are confirmed or still unknown? Act: Confirm transport and receiving capability with medical professionals, then pass on observed changes, care given, medication and ongoing hazards without diagnosing from the image. Simulated training scene \| 9.8 Clinic access and receiving capability. Observe: Which apparent delays involve registration, language, payment or limited medical resources, and what details need checking directly? Act: Keep the casualty supported, contact emergency services and confirm the receiving facility and transport arrangements; do not delay urgent care simply to complete paperwork. ### A handover must explain how a casualty changed A visitor walks after a nearby explosion, then becomes unusually drowsy thirty minutes later. Another has increasing difficulty breathing while being transported. Saying only “the person is injured” hides crucial information. Tell the receiving clinicians when and how the injury occurred; what breathing and consciousness were like initially; how they have changed; whether there is severe bleeding; and what care has been given. Avoid presenting unconfirmed diagnoses as facts. Check whether the clinic can treat the presenting injuries or arrange an appropriate transfer. Obtain appropriate professional guidance about emergency transfer and the actual receiving facility. ## Module-specific assessment A person walks after a blast but becomes drowsy, while another has major visible bleeding. Describe how to protect rescuers, recognise urgent changes and deliver useful information to professional responders. Identify which skills require supervised practical training. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, read the explanations and revisit the specific skill behind each missed question. [Open quiz.ravenlong.com online quiz \| 15 questions →](https://quiz.ravenlong.com/en/09/)

modules.title: 10 | Emergency Communications, Crisis Response, and Evacuation
modules.body: Module 10 \| Emergency Communications, Crisis Response and Evacuation A crisis may involve missing people, failed equipment, urgent medical needs and stopped operations at the same time. Learn to pass actionable information, account for personnel and make shelter or evacuation decisions. Learning outcome: Deliver a concise incident report, support an orderly response and confirm safety before operations resume. ## 10.1 \| Use communications that survive the incident Emergency communications must also work during outages, overloads and confiscation. Coverage may be absent, networks overloaded, communications restricted or devices confiscated. These failures require different responses. For an unavoidable remote visit, a lawfully permitted satellite phone, two-way satellite messenger or trained use of appropriate radio equipment may help. Test actual transmission, service activation, battery and receipt. Agree in advance which channel will be used, who receives each message and how local support will be requested. A person taken into an undisclosed detention facility may have no equipment at all. A complete plan therefore has two parts: how the traveller reports while communication remains available, and what trusted people outside can independently do if direct contact becomes impossible. The second part must be arranged before departure. Simulated training scene \| 10.1 Vehicle breakdown on a remote road without mobile coverage (additional scenario). Observe: With the vehicle immobilised and phones offline, what traffic, terrain, weather and personnel hazards need assessment? Act: Protect passengers without increasing roadside exposure. Use a pre-tested, locally lawful satellite or radio channel to report location, headcount, the breakdown and assistance needed. Do not walk blindly into unfamiliar terrain to search for a mobile signal. ## 10.2 \| Recognise when immediate response is needed When an update is late, check the expected coverage, last contact and planned activity. A delayed meeting, a late vehicle or a known no-coverage section may explain the silence. By contrast, witnessing an armed removal, the forcible seizure of a phone or a person being taken to an unknown facility is evidence that cannot reasonably be treated as a routine late check-in. For ordinary delays, verify the person's last message, companions and destination according to the agreed process. For direct evidence of restraint or violence, protect the people still at the scene and start appropriate external assistance promptly. Direct evidence of coercion or violence triggers immediate external assistance. A witness should get to a safer location, preserve the last observed facts and contact the agreed receiver. They can reach a safer location, preserve what they personally saw and provide that information to the agreed receiver and competent support channels. Simulated training scene \| 10.2 Priorities under an immediate threat. Observe: Can you establish the threat direction, exposed personnel and usable protective positions? Which facts remain unconfirmed? Action: During gunfire or another immediate threat, stop exposed work and take protective action under the site's emergency procedure. Only when it does not increase exposure, send a short report stating location, observed threat and known casualties. Do not delay protection to complete written reporting. ### Immediate action and external coordination An explosion, building fire and witnessed detention require different people to act in different ways. Immediate threats to life call for protective action without waiting for a formal reply. When a person is taken away and cannot communicate, the external receiver should start the identity-verification and lawful tracing process. A workable arrangement states what events end the activity immediately, what direct evidence must be preserved, and which lawful channels an external helper should activate. Write the actions, triggers and responsibilities into the plan before departure. ## 10.3 \| Report only information that enables action “Someone has disappeared. Please help” conveys urgency but gives little information that an embassy or lawyer can use. A useful first report identifies the traveller and nationality, last directly confirmed place and time, the stated purpose of the visit, what witnesses actually saw, the last message, what is unknown and the specific assistance requested. For example: “A visitor holding a passport from \[country\] was seen being taken from \[historic site\] at 14:20 by individuals identifying themselves as officials. Their last personal message was at 14:12. The agency and place of detention are unconfirmed. Secure identity and lawful visit documents are available. Please assist with identity and custody enquiries.” Save the time and channel of the report and any acknowledgement. Subsequent updates should state verified changes with one agreed, factual incident record. Share identity copies only through trusted official channels. ### A first report must prevent a search from becoming confused One witness says “someone was arrested”, another says “I heard they were kidnapped”, and a third tells the family “we found the prison.” All may refer to the same incident without supporting the same conclusion. Write the last independently confirmed time and location, what the people taking the person identified themselves as, the direction of transfer if seen, and when communication was lost. Label anything else unconfirmed. Verify custody information through the relevant legal and official channels. Protect sensitive identity data from uncontrolled sharing and provide full materials only through appropriate consular, legal or authorised channels. ## 10.4 \| Understand decision-making roles A missing-person response can involve several groups at the same time. A companion knows the last witnessed facts. A pre-agreed receiver holds identity records and coordinates updates. A local Fixer or interpreter may understand administrative pathways. A qualified lawyer and consular authorities provide their respective formal assistance. These responsibilities should not collapse into “ask a local friend to sort it out.” The witness protects remaining travellers and records facts. The receiver maintains one reliable evidence record. A Fixer may lawfully verify site arrangements, translate and assist with permitted enquiries, while legal decisions and formal approaches stay with qualified professionals. Legal and consular professionals should assess formal access and identity verification. Independent travellers can nominate a trusted receiver and find competent local support before departure. ## 10.5 \| Account for people and casualties Account for people by name and verified status. Six visitors set out; five return. The missing person's last device location is still near the site. Only five people are confirmed safe. Keep the sixth person's status open until direct or reliable confirmation is available. Record each person as directly confirmed safe, confirmed injured, confirmed under restraint or not yet confirmed. Preserve the last verified contact and eyewitness account, noting gaps in the record instead of filling them with assumptions. If a person was taken away, the remaining companions must not endanger themselves trying to follow. Maintain the status as unconfirmed until credible evidence establishes where the person is and whether they are safe. Credible personal confirmation or appropriate verified institutional information is needed. ### External response when somebody is taken away and disappears This process applies to witnessed detention, suspected unacknowledged custody and an unexplained disappearance that has crossed the agreed escalation threshold. Assign one person to maintain the case record and coordinate updates. Keep one verified case record while allowing formal consular, legal and emergency channels to work in parallel. | Action | Who can perform it | Useful result | | --- | --- | --- | | Protect those still at the scene | Companions and site staff | Other people reach a safer position; time and place of the removal are recorded | | Assemble proof of identity | Pre-agreed external receiver | Secure passport, nationality, entry permissions, travel purpose and relevant identity details | | Contact the embassy/consulate | Receiver, family or authorised person | Formal notification, acknowledgement and clear request to verify custody or location | | Begin lawful local enquiries | Qualified lawyer, suitable Fixer/interpreter | Check appropriate official, immigration or detention channels without declaring rumours confirmed | | Maintain a case record | Named coordinator | Witness accounts, responses, uncertainties and follow-up dates kept together | | Arrange safe handover when found | Appropriate consular, legal and medical support | Confirmed identity, health needs, documents and onward care | Embassies can assist with identity verification, contact requests and consular communication. In unstable regions, local legal and administrative procedures may take time, so the external receiver should maintain accurate records and follow up through the appropriate channels. Consider a visitor held for an extended period without an obvious public procedure. Later, contact with people managing the holding site and verification involving consular and immigration authorities makes it possible to establish identity and arrange release. The case shows the value of supplying accurate identity and last-sighting records early to lawful and competent authorities. ### Recording last contact, last sighting and new evidence The person last sends a direct message at 14:12. At 14:20 a companion sees them enter a vehicle under constraint. At 14:25 their phone becomes unreachable. These are three different facts: the person's own message, the witness account and the device status. Combining them into “they vanished at 14:25 at the site” can distort the most important timeline. Record direct confirmation, reliable witnessing, old device location and unknown status separately. The agreed GOTWA Actions arrangement allows an external receiver to submit identity and witness information even when the detainee's phone is unavailable. Keep witnesses in a safe place and pass their evidence to the external receiver. ## 10.6 \| Choose shelter, relocation or evacuation Sheltering and evacuation solve different problems. If armed violence is taking place outside while a building remains usable, rushing into the street may increase exposure. If smoke, fire or structural damage develops inside, the same building may no longer be an appropriate refuge. A traveller may not have access to a corporate safe haven. A staffed, usable location can offer temporary protection if it is genuinely accessible and the situation permits. Check whether the intended shelter can receive you before moving. Follow lawful access arrangements. When a person is held at an unknown location, their priority is survival and essential health. The external receiver and legal or consular contacts handle tracing and access requests. The plan should name who carries out each task. ### Shelter, local relocation and regional evacuation solve different problems Gunfire outside a hotel may make running into an open entrance unsafe while the building remains usable. Smoke entering the same building may make continued sheltering dangerous. Remaining within protected space, moving to another nearby safe location and leaving a wider region involve different hazards, permissions and resources. Short-term visitors may have no dedicated safe house or protected fleet. Confirm that the alternative location is open, reachable and able to receive the group. Contact the embassy through its official channels to confirm practical reception arrangements. ## 10.7 \| Complete movement and handover during evacuation Evacuation requires more than a waiting vehicle. Travellers need an actually usable exit, transport suited to their condition, a lawful route and somewhere able to receive them. During unrest, the pickup vehicle may be several streets away while a companion is unable to walk. Moving through a confrontation simply to reach transport may make the situation worse. Casualties may need professional medical transport and care during the journey. Keep detained and unconfirmed people listed separately in the personnel record. Account for everyone again at each receiving location. The operation is complete only when people are genuinely received, medical needs have been handed over and outstanding missing-person enquiries have an owner. ## 10.8 \| Recover safely and learn from the incident Once the immediate danger ends, arrange health care, documentation and any longer-term support. A person held for weeks may need medical attention, nutrition, sleep, legal help and psychological support. Witnesses may also be distressed. A return to sightseeing or work should not be the first obligation imposed on the person. A meaningful review asks whether witnesses kept the last directly verified location, whether the external receiver held adequate identity records, and whether local and consular enquiries were given accurate information early enough. Identify control failures and improvements and turn the findings into specific corrections. When serious wrongdoing may have occurred, preserve factual records and seek suitable professional assistance without forcing repeated accounts from someone who is not ready to provide them. Two-image observation exercise (both are simulated training scenes): Image one tests personnel accounting: Can a single image prove that everyone is safe, casualties have received care and the missing worker has been found? Action: complete headcounts, injury checks and missing-person follow-up before full recovery. Image two tests restart conditions: Can the image establish that access controls, equipment and surrounding threats are acceptable? Action: inspect protection and equipment, record gaps and obtain an authorised phased restart decision; maintain restrictions until verified. ## Module-specific assessment At 14:12 a visitor sends a direct message; at 14:20 someone sees them being taken away; at 14:25 the phone becomes unreachable. Produce an initial report that keeps those facts distinct. Compare GOTWA actions for witnessed detention and for an expected gap in mobile coverage. ## Module quiz \| 15 questions After submitting, read the explanations and revisit the specific skill behind each missed question. modules.body: Lesson 11 \| Integrated HEAT Review: Three High-Risk Situations The review brings the ten modules together through practical decisions. The review uses three continuous cases: an operational worksite, a short-term visitor taken into unknown custody, and an incident of escalating unrest during a public visit. Learners must explain why apparently sensible actions may actually increase exposure. ## Integrated scenario A \| A worksite under changing conditions Before reviewing the first incident, remember that you can control your actions and the protection actually available to youas conditions change around you. A response that makes sense in one situation can become dangerous when the source of harm changes. ## One decision sequence across the course Identify the immediate danger, stop actions that increase exposure, take practical protection, account for people, and reassess movement or resumption as facts change. Different hazards require different first actions. ### Stage 1｜Before work begins You and four colleagues enter a worksite in an area affected by armed activity. The task is electrical maintenance. Before entry, confirm scope, personnel, protective equipment, alarm procedures, internal protected areas and medical capability. Question: One worker has not received the site alarm briefing. Can that person start work and be trained later? Review answer No. Complete the necessary briefing before exposure. The worker must know how to stop work, take protection and respond to an emergency assembly requirement. ### Stage 2｜Noticing an abnormal change The morning is quiet. In the afternoon nearby shops close unexpectedly, unfamiliar vehicles stop outside the entrance and people repeatedly watch the site. Question: Does this prove an attack is imminent? What should change now? Review answer No. Record the observed behaviour while keeping observations separate from assumptions. Pause unnecessary exposed work and verify the security situation. Do not go outside to confront unknown people. ### Stage 3｜A confrontation develops People gather and demand entry to the work area. A language misunderstanding causes an argument, and the gate begins to be pushed. Question: Should staff keep explaining the project or change the working arrangement? Review answer Suspend exposed activity and move non-essential staff away from the gate. Only authorised people should engage from a controlled position. Pushing, thrown objects or weapons shift the priority to protecting personnel. ### Stage 4｜Gunfire is heard Shots sound outside the worksite. Several workers run towards the gate to see what happened. Question: What is the first protective action? Review answer Stop exposed work, move away from gates, windows and open ground, and use a previously identified protective area. Do not approach the gunfire or expose yourself for footage. ### Stage 5｜Casualties occur During movement into the building, one colleague is cut by shattered glass and another has difficulty breathing. The threat outside has not ended. Question: Whom do you help first? Can everyone be moved immediately to vehicles outside? Review answer Start by confirming scene safety. Seek urgent medical help for life-threatening symptoms. Check responsiveness, breathing and severe bleeding. Do not send rescuers into ongoing danger; movement must consider the casualty and safe access. ### Stage 6｜Communications and headcount Network service fails. Four people have reached the internal protected area. The fifth remains unaccounted for. Question: Does a phone location near the building prove the missing worker is safe? Review answer No. Account for people by name. Use old location data as a search lead and keep the person's status unconfirmed. Use available emergency communications to report four confirmed and one unconfirmed. Do not send untrained staff back into danger. ### Stage 7｜Shelter or evacuate? Gunfire stops briefly but unknown people remain outside. The building is usable. Ten minutes later smoke begins entering it. Question: Should both situations trigger the same action? Review answer No. When danger is outside and the building still protects people, internal shelter may be appropriate. Smoke inside changes the hazard: reassess safe exits and follow relevant fire evacuation procedures. ### Stage 8｜Deciding to resume operations The incident appears to have ended. Management wants maintenance to restart, but access controls are damaged, a casualty has not been transferred and the missing worker is still unconfirmed. Question: Can the incident be closed and full work resume? Review answer No. Account for personnel, complete medical handover and assess the facility, equipment and affected work areas. An authorised person decides what can safely restart and addresses the control failures revealed by the event. ## Integrated scenario B \| A short-term visitor is taken away and cannot be traced Two visitors enter a historic site in a region affected by instability. At 14:12, one sends a message confirming entry into the public visitor area. At 14:20, their companion sees people identifying themselves as officials order the visitor into a vehicle. The witness does not see a formal custody record and cannot identify the receiving agency. Direct contact ceases, and no public detention information is available for weeks. The scenario must be considered from three distinct positions. You are the person taken away. When armed people are restricting your movements, avoid sudden physical resistance over documents or a phone. In an unknown holding location, focus on preserving life, food, water, hygiene, sleep and medical needs. If a safe opportunity arises, use simple local-language phrases to request interpretation, medical care and notification of your embassy. Lack of a response does not make a dangerous escape attempt a universal solution. You are the last witness. Move to safety and record what you observed as the person was taken away. First get yourself and remaining companions to safety. Write down the time, exact place, what you directly saw and the last confirmed personal message. Explicitly distinguish what you did not see. Give the record to the agreed external receiver instead of guessing where the detainee was taken. You are the external receiver or Fixer. Assemble secure identity copies, entry and visit permissions, companion information and the last verified location. Submit accurate facts and an assistance request to the person's embassy or consulate. Engage a suitable lawyer and lawful local channels in parallel, preserving acknowledgements and separating unverified leads. A Fixer handles translation and lawful local coordination; the lawyer and consular officer manage their respective formal procedures. Suppose that, after an extended period, lawful contact with people managing the holding location allows the person's identity to be checked through consular and immigration channels, leading to release. Arrange safe reception and health assessment first. Travel plans can be revisited afterward. Legal documentation and follow-up come afterward. Review question: If the original handover said only “return by 18:00”, what evidence would outside helpers lack at 14:20? How would a complete GOTWA Actions plan make the response possible without the detainee's phone? --- ## Integrated scenario C \| A public visit disrupted by unrest Three short-term visitors are visiting a public exhibition in a city affected by instability. The morning is normal, with staff at the entrance and transport access nearby. At 2:30 p.m., a gathering begins in the square. People chant while police direct traffic. The exhibition remains open. At this stage, remain inside the protected venue and stop filming from the entrance. Fifteen minutes later, pushing and thrown objects appear. Staff close the main entrance and direct visitors to wait inside. The driver reports that the vehicle cannot reach its usual pickup point and suggests walking through an unfamiliar alley to another street. One visitor has sprained an ankle and cannot walk quickly. The group now needs to check the building's protection, usable exits, the suggested alley and the injured visitor's ability to move. If the pickup vehicle cannot reach the venue, compare safe waiting with an approved alternative route. Then a fire alarm sounds inside the building. Someone smells smoke and staff direct occupants towards another staircase. The source of danger has changed. The fire alarm changes the decision: reassess safe exits and how the group can leave. Eventually the group reaches a different venue that has confirmed it can receive them. The response is complete after every person has been accounted for, health needs checked and onward arrangements updated. Try these decisions before reading the review: 1. Which observations would justify staying inside the venue during the early gathering? 2. What would you need to know before using the suggested alley with an injured companion? 3. What makes the internal smoke hazard different from the external crowd threat? 4. Can a phone's old location at the exhibition establish that all three visitors are safe? Review: The incident begins with crowd exposure, failed transport access and an injured companion, then develops into an internal fire hazard. Initially, remaining inside a protective venue while checking transport arrangements may be the safer option. Smoke inside changes the shelter decision. All people must be directly accounted for before the response can be considered complete. ## Before the final assessment 1. Can you distinguish direct observations from unconfirmed information? 2. Can you explain the first protective action and why another tempting action increases exposure? 3. Can you say when to stop work, when to shelter or evacuate, and when operations must not resume? 4. Can you distinguish a confirmed safe person from an indirect clue? Hands-on bleeding control, complex first aid and specialist protective driving require supervised practical training.
